title: staircase-ramp-throughput-notes
content:
Experiment log: staircase ramp (step-increase) load profile

Goal:
- Understand steady-state latency and p99 behavior when increasing offered load in discrete steps (staircase). Identify transition effects (cache coldness, batching penalties) and whether autoscaling or routing policies introduce transient spikes.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Environment: Dedicated dev cluster (4x A100-80GB), serving runtime build: v2.14.0-rc3 (kv-cache fixes not applied). Model: textron-7b-q4 (quantized, 16k KV cache). Sequence length: 512 tokens. Request mix: 60% short prompts (~64 tokens), 40% long completions (~512 tokens).
- Load pattern: stairs at 0 -> 200 -> 400 -> 800 -> 1200 -> 1600 QPS; each step 10 minutes with 5 minute warmup, total run ~1.25 hours. Concurrency target derived from QPS and avg latency.
- Findings:
  * p50 largely linear with load until 1200 QPS; p95 and p99 show step-transition spikes at the moment of QPS increase (30s-90s), p99 up to 3x baseline at peaks.
  * Major root cause appears to be KV cache cold misses and request reserialization during worker pool adjustments (we observe high kernel latency on first requests after step change).
  * Batching timeout (default 5ms) led to increased tail during step changes; reducing to 2ms reduced p99 spike magnitude by ~30% but increased CPU pressure.
  * Autoscaler (scale-up-on-queue) reacts after ~45s, but the initial p99 spike is before capacity adds take effect.

Detailed notes:
- Commands used:
  * loadgen: benchgen --pattern staircase --steps 0,200,400,800,1200,1600 --step-duration 600s --concurrency auto --p95-goal 250ms --seed 20251108
  * serving node traces: curl http://node-2.local:6060/debug/trace | gzip > step2-trace-800.gz

- Observed metrics (representative):
  Step 200 QPS: throughput tokens/s ~ 78k, p50 42ms, p95 118ms, p99 210ms
  Step 400 QPS: tokens/s ~ 156k, p50 48ms, p95 140ms, p99 270ms
  Step 800 QPS: tokens/s ~ 308k, p50 55ms, p95 180ms, p99 540ms (transient spike first 60s to 3x)
  Step 1200 QPS: tokens/s ~ 460k, p50 72ms, p95 230ms, p99 900ms (spike during scale events)
  Step 1600 QPS: cluster saturated, sustained queue growth, p50 110ms, p95 410ms, p99 >1500ms and many timeouts (client 10s).

- Tracing/Profiling observations:
  * KV cache hit rate drops at step transitions from ~98% steady to ~65% briefly; explains additional forward passes and attention recompute.
  * Worker process metrics show GC/deserialization stalls when dev-allocations increase; serialized payload deserial step takes ~20-50ms on spikes.
  * GPU utilization jumps but not uniformly: one node shows 95% while others 65%, indicating uneven routing/burst packing.

Quick experiments tried mid-run:
- Reduce batch timeout to 2ms: rerun step 800 for 10m: p99 spike magnitude reduced by ~30%, p95 improved ~12%, CPU sys jumps +18%.
- Pre-warm KV cache by injecting synthetic prefix requests before step increase: p99 spike almost eliminated for short bursts but cost >10% extra tokens (not sustainable).
- Disable autoscaler (manual capacity) and ramp slowly: tail improved but unrealistic for production elasticity needs.

Interpretation / hypothesis:
- Transition spikes are multi-factor: KV cache transient misses + batching dynamics + worker serialization overhead + imperfect routing leading to node-level hotspots. Autoscaler is too slow to prevent initial tail; batching timeout tradeoffs mean lowering timeouts helps tail but increases CPU cost.

Actionable next steps:
1) Reproduce with the v2.14.1 build (includes recent kv-cache cold hit mitigation) to see if cache churn reduces.
2) Add a small pre-step micro-warmup (10% added QPS for 30s) to measure cost vs tail benefit; automate as a routing policy option for canary rollouts.
3) Instrument deserialization path and move heavy work off request lane (async unpack + pooling). File a PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/??
4) Explore adaptive batch timeout: dynamic timeout that shrinks on step-up events for 15-30s window, then relaxes back. Prototype suggested config in bench-scripts.
5) Update autoscaler policy to consider gradient-of-arrival (ramp detection) to pre-emptively spin up capacity when slope > threshold.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Cost tradeoff for pre-warming: quantify extra tokens vs SLA improvement for typical customer workloads.
- Is there an inexpensive signal to detect impending global load step from LB or edge collector earlier? (edge QPS derivative?)
- Confirm whether deserialization stall is due to Python pickle/unpickle or our request wrapper; try native msgpack pipeline in a follow-up run.

Notes to self / rough checklist:
- [ ] Run same staircase with v2.14.1 (kv-cache patch) (assigned: Ravi)
- [ ] Add micro-warmup toggle to benchgen and test cost delta (assigned: Marta)
- [ ] Add detailed flamegraph for deserialization on node-2 (assigned: Isabel)
- [ ] Draft proposal for adaptive batch timeout (short doc)

Attachments I saved during run:
- step2-trace-800.gz (trace)
- node-2-flame-20251108.svg (flamegraph)
- bench-output/staircase-20251108.csv (raw metrics)

Notes: keep this in users/ until results reproducible and we have v2.14.1 comparison. Will move to shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime when ready for team review.

End of scratchpad.
